challenges.name: cache-aside-ttl-quiz
challenges.title: Cache-aside timelines
challenges.description: Two timelines from the enrollment campaign: course keys warmed together at a deploy, and a negative-cache entry for a course that was published a few seconds later.

questions.question:
The deploy at 10:00:00 warmed the 500 most-viewed courses with SET course:<id> <json> EX 300. At 10:01:53:

$ for id in c_12 c_13 c_14 c_15; do redis-cli TTL course:$id; done
(integer) 187
(integer) 187
(integer) 187
(integer) 187

pg_stat_statements, calls per minute of the course lookup:
10:04  410
10:05  23,900
10:06  380
10:09  395
10:10  24,100

Statement: "Storing each course with EX 300 plus a random 0 to 60 seconds would turn these spikes into misses spread over about a minute."
questions.explanation: True. All 500 keys were written within the same second with the same TTL, so they expire within the same second (TTL 187 on every key) and the misses reach PostgreSQL together, every 300 seconds. With a random 0-60 s added per key, keys written together expire at different moments across a 61-second window; once reloaded they get new random TTLs, so the waves do not line up again. Lowering the TTL would only make the spikes more frequent. Note what jitter does not do: it spreads many keys apart, but it does not protect a single very hot key from many concurrent misses (a stampede, lesson 11). The misconception is that the TTL value is the problem; the problem is that the expiry times are identical.

questions.question:
getCourse caches "not found" as the JSON null for 30 seconds and courses for 300 + jitter. Nothing invalidates the cache when an admin publishes a course. redis-cli MONITOR and the admin log:

10:00:05.120 "GET" "course:c_207"
10:00:05.124 "SET" "course:c_207" "null" "EX" "30"      (learner A: 404)
10:00:20.000 admin publishes c_207 (INSERT committed in PostgreSQL)
10:00:31.870 "GET" "course:c_207"                        (learner B: 404)

Statement: "Learner C, who opens /courses/c_207 at 10:00:40, also gets a 404, because the not-found entry lasts 30 seconds from the moment the course was published."
questions.explanation: False. A TTL counts from the command that set it, here the SET at 10:00:05.124, so the not-found entry expires at 10:00:35.124. Redis knows nothing about the INSERT in PostgreSQL at 10:00:20. Learner B at 10:00:31 was still inside the 30 seconds and got the cached 404; learner C at 10:00:40 misses the cache, getCourse loads c_207 from PostgreSQL and returns it (and caches it with the normal TTL). The worst case for a newly published course is therefore the negative TTL after the last not-found answer, which is why the negative TTL is kept short. The misconception is that cache expiry is related to when the data changed in the database; without invalidation the two are independent.

challenges.name: cache-aside-get-course
challenges.title: Cache-aside for course pages
challenges.description: GET /courses/:id on CodeDev reads PostgreSQL on every request. Write getCourse(id, deps) with cache-aside on the in-memory Redis model (deps.redis, a FakeRedis on a fake clock) in front of the fake database (deps.db). Key: "course:<id>". On a hit, return the cached course parsed from JSON - or null for a cached "not found" - without calling deps.db. On a miss, call deps.db.findCourseById(id) once and store the result: a found course as JSON.stringify(course) with a TTL (in whole seconds) of COURSE_TTL_SECONDS + Math.floor(deps.random() * (COURSE_TTL_JITTER_SECONDS + 1)), that is 300 to 360 s; call deps.random() exactly once per stored course and never otherwise. A course that does not exist (null) is stored as a not-found marker of your choice (the JSON "null" works) for NOT_FOUND_TTL_SECONDS (30 s). When findCourseById throws (database down), let the error propagate and write nothing to Redis. A cached value that is not valid JSON (an older deploy wrote it) counts as a miss: load and overwrite it. FakeRedis.set(key, value, { ex }) rejects an EX that is not a positive whole number, like Redis. Input (JSON on stdin): { db: Course[], random: number[], steps }. The runner replays the steps - get, advance (ms), ttl, dbUpsert, dbRemove, dbDown, dbUp, corrupt - printing one line per get (the course as JSON, null, or error: <message>) and per ttl, then a last line with the database reads and the Redis GET and SET counts.
hints: Three different things can come back from Redis for course:<id> - nothing, a course, or your not-found marker - and three from the database - a course, null, or an exception. Which of these six cases should end with a write to Redis, and with which TTL?

Look at the order of operations in getCourse: the Redis read, the parse (which can throw on a value from an older deploy), the database call (which can throw when it is down) and the set with { ex }. Only the parse error should be caught; the database error must leave the function before any set. And the TTL passed to ex must be an integer.

A similar case on other data: caching a learner's public profile under "profile:<userId>" with a base TTL of 600 s and up to 120 s of jitter. With random() = 0.25 the TTL is 600 + Math.floor(0.25 * 121) = 630. A missing profile is stored as "null" for 20 s; a timeout from the profile table stores nothing and is rethrown, so the request after recovery reads the table again.
